options.label: B
options.text: A protein product derived from collagen (found in animal connective tissue, bones, skin), hydrolyzed to extract

questions.question: Commercial culinary gelatin comes primarily in two forms:

options.label: B
options.text: Powdered (dry powder) and sheet/leaf gelatin (thin transparent sheets)

questions.question: Sheet (leaf) gelatin vs. powdered gelatin conversion depends on bloom strength (gel strength), but roughly:

options.label: B
options.text: 1 standard sheet (approx. 2.5 g) ≈ 3 g (about 1 tsp) of powdered gelatin (check the package bloom rating)

questions.question: Before adding gelatin to a hot liquid (base), it must be bloomed (hydrated), which means:

options.label: B
options.text: Sprinkling it over cold liquid (usually 5× its weight in water or the recipe liquid) and letting it sit for 5–10 minutes to absorb fluid and swell (no lumps)

options.label: D
options.text: Adding it directly to boiling liquid

questions.question: Why must gelatin not be boiled after it has been added to the base?

options.label: B
options.text: Boiling breaks down the protein structure, destroying its gelling ability (it won't set)

questions.question: The correct temperature range to dissolve bloomed gelatin into a base is:

options.label: B
options.text: Warm to hot but NOT boiling (ideally 104–122 °F / 40–50 °C minimum to dissolve; stay under a boil once dissolved)

questions.question: Gelatin sets (gels) when cooled to approximately:

options.label: B
options.text: Below 68 °F (20 °C); ideally refrigerated below 40 °F (4 °C) for a firm set; melts again above about 95 °F (35 °C)

questions.question: Foods containing raw pineapple, kiwi, papaya, or figs (which contain proteolytic enzymes such as bromelain) will not set with gelatin unless:

options.label: B
options.text: The fruits are first cooked (heat inactivates the enzymes that break down gelatin protein)

questions.question: A basic ratio for a firm gelatin dessert or mold (aspic) is approximately:

options.label: B
options.text: 1 oz (28 g) powdered gelatin per quart (liter) of liquid for a firm set; less for softer, spoonable textures

questions.question: Vegetarian/vegan alternatives to animal-based gelatin include:

options.label: B
options.text: Agar-agar (seaweed derivative), pectin (fruit), carrageenan, or vegan "gelatin" powders (carrageenan/guar gum blends)

options.label: C
options.text: Cornstarch only (doesn't give a true gel)

questions.question: Agar-agar differs from gelatin in that it:

options.label: B
options.text: Sets at a much higher temperature (around 85 °F / 35 °C vs. gelatin's melt) and does not require refrigeration to set (sets at room temperature)

options.label: D
options.text: Is clear and flavorless only (both can be)

questions.question: When making a savory jelly (aspic) for garnish or coating (chaud-froid):

options.label: B
options.text: Dissolve bloomed gelatin in warm flavored stock (consommé or seasoned stock), coat items while the liquid is still liquid but cooling, then chill to set

questions.question: If a gelatin mixture "weeps" (separates and releases liquid) after setting, possible causes are:

options.label: B
options.text: Over-stirring while setting, temperature fluctuations (slight melting), or an incorrect gelatin-to-liquid ratio

questions.question: In culinary terms, extraction refers specifically to:

options.label: B
options.text: The process of drawing out flavors, colors, nutrients, and gelatin from solid ingredients (bones, vegetables, aromatics) into a liquid medium (water) through simmering

questions.question: The primary agents that drive extraction in stock making are:

options.label: B
options.text: Time, temperature (simmering, not boiling), and the surface area of the solids (cutting or smashing bones)

questions.question: Why should stock be simmered gently rather than boiled vigorously during extraction?

options.label: B
options.text: Vigorous boiling creates turbidity (cloudiness), emulsifies fat improperly, and can make the stock bitter or greasy; a gentle simmer allows slow, clear extraction

questions.question: Blanching bones before making white stock affects extraction by:

options.label: B
options.text: Removing impurities (blood, scum) that would cloud the stock, resulting in cleaner extraction of flavors later

questions.question: Roasting bones before brown stock affects extraction by:

options.label: B
options.text: The Maillard reaction develops deeper, richer flavors (caramelized sugars and proteins) that then extract into the liquid, and adds color to the final stock

options.label: D
options.text: Making extraction faster (it actually takes the same time)

questions.question: Cutting or smashing marrow bones before making stock improves extraction because it:

options.label: B
options.text: Increases surface area, allowing water better access to extract marrow fats and collagen/gelatin from inside the bone

questions.question: Mirepoix (onion, carrot, celery) added to stocks aids extraction by:

options.label: B
options.text: Providing additional soluble sugars, aromatic compounds, and subtle sweetness and flavor depth that extract into the liquid

questions.question: The cold-start method (starting bones in cold water and bringing them to a simmer together) aids extraction by:

options.label: B
options.text: Allowing proteins to coagulate slowly and rise gently as scum, rather than seizing instantly, resulting in clearer stock with better removal of impurities to be skimmed

questions.question: Stock should not be over-reduced during initial extraction because:

options.label: B
options.text: Concentrated impurities and overly intense flavors may become bitter, and too high a salt concentration can inhibit further gentle extraction of delicate flavors

questions.question: Straining through a chinois at the end of extraction ensures:

options.label: B
options.text: Removal of all exhausted solids (spent bones, mirepoix, sachet), leaving only the extracted clear, flavorful liquid

questions.question: Reduction in cooking is defined as:

options.label: B
options.text: Simmering or boiling a liquid to evaporate water, thereby concentrating flavors, thickness, and intensity

questions.question: The primary purposes of reduction include all EXCEPT:

options.label: D
options.text: Adding volume or diluting the sauce (reduction removes volume)

questions.question: When reducing a sauce, if you reduce it too much (too far or too fast):

options.label: B
options.text: It may become overly salty (salt doesn't evaporate), bitter (caramelized sugars burn), too thick or gluey, or the color darkens excessively

questions.question: Deglazing is closely related to reduction because it:

options.label: B
options.text: Dissolves fond (brown, flavorful bits from sautéing or searing) into the liquid, which is then reduced to concentrate those flavors into the sauce

questions.question: A glace (meat glaze) is created by:

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing brown stock (or espagnole) by about three-quarters (75%) or more until it heavily coats a spoon, a highly concentrated, paint-like consistency

questions.question: When reducing acidic liquids (wine, vinegar, citrus juices) for sauces:

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce extremely fast over high heat

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce gently; acids can become harsh or bitter if reduced too aggressively (volatile compounds concentrate sharply); a pinch of sugar can help balance

questions.question: Flash reduction (rapid boiling to reduce quickly) is appropriate when:

options.label: B
options.text: You need to reduce a large volume quickly to save time, or when making a syrup or glaze where caramelization of natural sugars is desired (as opposed to slow reduction for clarity)

questions.question: Properly stopping or finalizing a reduction at the desired consistency is done by:

options.label: B
options.text: Removing it from heat, possibly finishing with cold butter or cream (monté au beurre), or transferring it to a bain-marie to hold without continuing to cook or reduce

questions.question: Evaporation rate during reduction is affected by:

options.label: B
options.text: Surface area of the liquid (wider pans evaporate faster), temperature (higher is faster), and air movement (ventilation)

questions.question: When reducing a cream-based sauce (which already contains milk solids):

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce uncovered over high heat, aggressively

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce gently and uncovered over low-to-medium heat; high heat can cause milk proteins to coagulate (graininess) or separate (breaking)
